title.en: Section 1 - A conversation about enrolling in a cooking class
title.zh: 第一部分 - 关于报名烹饪课程的对话

sections.passage: A conversation between a prospective student, Rachel, and the administrator of the Culinary Arts School, Mark. Rachel is interested in enrolling in a cooking course to improve her skills before she opens her own restaurant. Mark explains that the school offers several courses at different levels. The Beginners' Course runs for six weeks on Tuesday evenings from 6 PM to 9 PM and costs 300 pounds. The Intermediate Course runs for eight weeks on Wednesday evenings and costs 450 pounds. The Advanced Professional Course, which is a full-time programme running for twelve weeks, Monday to Friday, costs 3,500 pounds. Rachel is most interested in the Advanced Professional Course because she wants to develop her skills quickly. The course covers a wide range of cuisines including French, Italian, Japanese, and Thai cooking, as well as pastry and baking techniques. Students also learn about menu planning, food hygiene, and kitchen management. Mark explains that the next intake begins on September 3rd and that places are limited to 16 students per class to ensure personalised attention. Each student has their own fully equipped cooking station. Rachel asks about the qualifications she will receive upon completion. Mark tells her that she will receive a Level 3 Diploma in Professional Cookery, which is recognised by the Craft Guild of Chefs. She will also have the opportunity to complete a two-week work placement at a local restaurant. To apply, Rachel needs to fill out an application form, provide two references, and attend a short interview. The application deadline is August 15th, and a deposit of 500 pounds is required to secure a place.

title.en: Section 2 - A talk about a community garden project
title.zh: 第二部分 - 关于社区花园项目的介绍

sections.passage: A presentation by Claire Thompson about the Greenfield Community Garden, a volunteer-run project that was established three years ago on a disused industrial site in the city centre. Claire, who is the project coordinator, explains that the garden covers approximately 2,000 square metres and includes 80 individual allotments, a communal herb garden, a children's growing area, and a small orchard with 30 fruit trees. The project currently has 120 active members who pay an annual membership fee of 30 pounds, which covers the cost of seeds, tools, and water. The garden is open every day from dawn until dusk, and members can access their allotments at any time during these hours. Claire describes the community events that take place throughout the year, including a spring planting festival in April, a summer barbecue in July, a harvest celebration in September, and a Christmas market in December. She highlights that the garden won the Green City Award last year for its contribution to urban greening and community wellbeing. Claire also discusses the educational workshops offered at the garden, which cover topics such as organic gardening techniques, composting, and wildlife-friendly planting. These workshops are open to both members and non-members, with non-members paying a small fee of 5 pounds per session. Claire mentions that the garden is looking for new volunteers to help with maintenance, particularly for watering during the summer months and general upkeep during the winter. She encourages interested individuals to visit the garden's website or speak to her directly after the presentation.

title.en: Section 3 - Two students discussing their coursework on urban planning
title.zh: 第三部分 - 两名学生讨论城市规划课程作业

sections.passage: A conversation between two undergraduate students, Olivia and Daniel, who are working on a joint assignment for their Urban Planning module. They have been asked to evaluate the success of a pedestrianisation scheme in a European city. They have chosen to study the case of Copenhagen, Denmark, which has progressively pedestrianised parts of its city centre since the 1960s. Olivia has gathered data showing that Copenhagen's main shopping street, Stroget, was one of the first major streets in Europe to be pedestrianised in 1962. Since then, the pedestrianised area has expanded significantly, and the city now has over 20 kilometres of car-free streets in its centre. Daniel has found research showing that pedestrianisation has had positive effects on both retail sales and property values. Shops in pedestrianised areas of Copenhagen have seen revenue increases of 25 to 40 percent compared to those on streets that remain open to traffic. Olivia mentions that the environmental benefits are also significant. Air quality in the pedestrianised zones has improved substantially, with nitrogen dioxide levels falling by approximately 40 percent. The number of cyclists in Copenhagen has also increased dramatically, with 62 percent of residents now commuting to work or school by bicycle. They discuss some of the challenges associated with pedestrianisation, including the need for reliable public transport alternatives and concerns from businesses about reduced accessibility for customers who drive. Daniel suggests they compare Copenhagen's approach with the pedestrianisation of Times Square in New York, which was initially controversial but has been widely regarded as a success. They decide to structure their report with an introduction, a literature review, case study analysis, and recommendations. They need to submit the assignment in three weeks, with a maximum word count of 3,000 words.

title.en: Section 4 - A lecture on the history of antibiotics
title.zh: 第四部分 - 关于抗生素历史的讲座

sections.passage: A university lecture by Professor Sarah Collins on the history and development of antibiotics. Professor Collins begins by explaining that the discovery of antibiotics is considered one of the most significant medical breakthroughs in history, saving an estimated 200 million lives since their introduction. The story begins in 1928, when Alexander Fleming, a Scottish bacteriologist working at St Mary's Hospital in London, noticed that a mould called Penicillium notatum had contaminated one of his petri dishes and was killing the bacteria around it. He published his findings in 1929, but it was not until 1940 that Howard Florey and Ernst Boris Chain at Oxford University successfully purified penicillin for medical use. Mass production of penicillin began during World War II, and it is estimated that the drug saved approximately 100,000 lives during the D-Day landings alone. The success of penicillin led to a golden age of antibiotic discovery between the 1940s and 1960s, during which most of the antibiotic classes still used today were discovered, including streptomycin, tetracycline, and erythromycin. However, Professor Collins explains that this golden age came to an end as pharmaceutical companies found it increasingly difficult to discover new classes of antibiotics. Since 1987, no entirely new class of antibiotics has been approved for use in humans. She then discusses the growing problem of antibiotic resistance, which occurs when bacteria evolve mechanisms to survive exposure to antibiotics. The WHO has warned that antibiotic resistance is one of the greatest threats to global health, with an estimated 1.27 million deaths directly attributable to drug-resistant infections in 2019. Professor Collins identifies the overuse and misuse of antibiotics in both human medicine and agriculture as the primary drivers of resistance. She concludes by discussing potential solutions, including the development of new antibiotics, the use of bacteriophages, which are viruses that infect and kill bacteria, and improved diagnostic techniques that can identify infections more quickly and accurately, reducing unnecessary antibiotic prescriptions.

sections.passage: Tea is the most widely consumed beverage in the world after water, with an estimated 3 billion cups drunk every day across the globe. The origins of tea can be traced back to ancient China, where legend has it that the Emperor Shen Nung discovered the drink in 2737 BC when tea leaves accidentally blew into his pot of boiling water. While this story is almost certainly mythical, archaeological evidence suggests that tea was consumed in China as early as the Han Dynasty, around 200 BC. Initially, tea was used primarily for medicinal purposes, valued for its stimulating properties and believed to aid digestion and improve concentration. During the Tang Dynasty, which ruled from 618 to 907 AD, tea drinking became a widespread social practice, and the first known book about tea, 'The Classic of Tea' by Lu Yu, was published around 760 AD. This comprehensive guide covered everything from the cultivation of tea plants to the proper methods of preparation and served. The practice of tea drinking spread from China to Japan in the ninth century, carried by Buddhist monks who had studied in China. The Japanese developed their own elaborate tea ceremony, known as chanoyu, which emphasised harmony, respect, purity, and tranquillity. Tea did not arrive in Europe until the early seventeenth century, when the Dutch East India Company began importing it from China. It quickly became fashionable among the wealthy classes, and by the mid-seventeenth century, tea houses had begun to appear in major European cities. In Britain, tea was initially an expensive luxury, but its popularity grew rapidly, and by the eighteenth century, it had become the national drink. The British East India Company played a central role in the global tea trade, and the company's attempts to maintain its monopoly on tea imports to Britain contributed to events such as the Boston Tea Party of 1773, which was a key moment in the lead-up to the American Revolution. In the nineteenth century, the British began cultivating tea in India and Ceylon, now Sri Lanka, to reduce their dependence on Chinese imports. Today, the largest tea-producing countries are China, India, Kenya, and Sri Lanka, which together account for approximately 75 percent of global production.

title.en: Passage 2 - The Psychology of Colour in Marketing
title.zh: 文章2 - 营销中的色彩心理学

sections.passage: Colour plays a crucial role in marketing and branding, influencing consumer perceptions, emotions, and purchasing decisions in ways that most people are not consciously aware of. Research in colour psychology has shown that up to 90 percent of snap judgements about products can be based on colour alone, making it one of the most powerful tools available to marketers. The relationship between colour and consumer behaviour is complex and varies significantly across cultures, but some general patterns have been identified through decades of research. Red is perhaps the most psychologically stimulating colour, associated with urgency, excitement, and passion. It has been shown to increase heart rate and create a sense of urgency, which is why it is commonly used in sale signs, clearance events, and call-to-action buttons on websites. Studies have found that red backgrounds can increase purchase intent by up to 20 percent for impulse buyers. Blue, on the other hand, is associated with trust, reliability, and calmness. It is the most popular colour for corporate brands, with over 50 percent of the world's top 100 companies using blue in their logos, including Facebook, Samsung, and Ford. Green is strongly associated with nature, health, and environmental consciousness. It has become the colour of choice for organic and eco-friendly brands, and research has shown that green packaging can increase consumers' perceptions of a product's healthiness by up to 30 percent. Yellow is used to grab attention and convey optimism and warmth, which is why it is commonly used in window displays and signage. However, excessive use of yellow can cause anxiety and visual fatigue. Black conveys sophistication, luxury, and exclusivity, which is why it is the dominant colour for premium brands such as Chanel, Prada, and Apple's product packaging. White suggests cleanliness, simplicity, and modernity, and has become increasingly popular in technology branding. The effectiveness of colour in marketing also depends on its context and appropriateness for the product category. Research has shown that the relationship between colour and product type is more important than the colour itself. For example, while warm colours such as red and orange tend to be more effective for food and beverage brands, cool colours such as blue and green are preferred for healthcare and financial services.

title.en: Passage 3 - Artificial Intelligence and Creative Arts
title.zh: 文章3 - 人工智能与创意艺术

sections.passage: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence has raised profound questions about the nature of creativity and whether machines can truly be creative. In recent years, AI systems have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in fields previously thought to be exclusively human, including visual art, music composition, poetry, and even screenwriting. In 2018, an AI-generated portrait titled 'Portrait of Edmond de Belamy' sold at Christie's auction house for 432,500 dollars, far exceeding its estimated price of 7,000 to 10,000 dollars. The portrait was created by a collective called Obvious using a type of AI known as a Generative Adversarial Network, which consists of two neural networks that work together to produce increasingly realistic outputs. In music, AI systems have been used to compose pieces in the style of famous composers. In 2019, researchers at Sony's Computer Science Laboratories used an AI system called Flow Machines to create a song in the style of the Beatles, which was played to audiences who were unable to distinguish it from a genuine Beatles composition. Google's Magenta project has developed AI tools that can generate original music across multiple genres, while OpenAI's MuseNet can compose music in the style of Mozart, Chopin, or any of dozens of other composers. However, many artists and philosophers argue that AI-generated art lacks the intentionality and emotional depth that characterise true creativity. They contend that AI systems do not understand the meaning of what they produce; they simply identify patterns in existing data and generate new combinations based on those patterns. The philosopher Margaret Boden distinguishes between three types of creativity: combinational creativity, which involves producing unfamiliar combinations of familiar ideas; exploratory creativity, which involves exploring the possibilities within a conceptual space; and transformational creativity, which involves fundamentally changing the rules of a conceptual space. Current AI systems are generally considered capable of the first two types but struggle with the third. The debate about AI and creativity also raises important questions about copyright and intellectual property. If an AI system creates a work of art, who owns the rights to it? Current legal frameworks in most countries do not recognise AI as a legal person capable of holding copyright, which creates significant uncertainty for the growing AI art market.
